6MWT, 6‐minute walk test; ABC, activities‐specific balance confidence; ADL, activities of daily living; BBS, Berg balance scale; BI, Barthel index; BWSTT, body weight‐supported treadmill training; E/C, experimental group/control group; EBWOWT, early body weight‐supported overground walking training; FAC, functional ambulation classification; FMA, Fugl‐Meyer assessment; FMB, Fugl‐Meyer balance; OGT, over‐ground training; RAGT, robot‐assisted gait training; RALT, robotic‐assisted locomotor training; RCT, randomized controlled trial; RMI, rivermead mobility index; RT, routine training; SET, sling exercise training; tDCS, transcranial direct current stimulation; TGT, treadmill gait training; TUGT, timed up and go test. 3.2. Quality Assessment The methodological quality assessment using the Cochrane risk‐of‐bias tool revealed varying levels of quality across the included studies (Figures 2 and 3 ). The majority of studies demonstrated low risk of bias in random sequence generation and allocation concealment. However, blinding of participants and personnel was challenging due to the nature of the interventions, resulting in a high risk of bias in this domain for most studies. Outcome assessment blinding was adequately performed in approximately half the studies. Most studies showed low risk of bias for incomplete outcome data and selective reporting. FIGURE 2 Risk of bias graph showing review authors' judgments about each risk of bias item presented as percentages across all included studies. The assessment covers random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. FIGURE 3 Risk of bias summary displaying review authors' judgments about each risk of bias item for each included study, presented as a detailed item‐by‐item assessment for all 23 included studies. 3.3. Effects of Interventions 3.3.1. Balance Function Thirteen studies evaluated the effect of SET on balance function using the BBS. Meta‐analysis revealed a significant improvement in balance function favoring the intervention group (SMD = 1.21, 95% CI: 0.61–1.81, p < 0.001). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed among these studies ( I 2 = 89.4%). This finding suggests that SET significantly enhances balance function in patients with stroke, although the magnitude of improvement varied considerably across studies (Figure 4 ). FIGURE 4 Forest plot showing the effect of SET on balance function in patients with stroke as measured by Berg Balance Scale (BBS). Meta‐analysis of 13 studies demonstrating overall effect size (SMD = 1.21, 95% CI: 0.61–1.81) with heterogeneity assessment ( I 2 = 89.4%, p < 0.001). 3.3.2. Activities of Daily Living Five studies assessed the impact on ADL. The pooled analysis showed a positive trend favoring SET, although the result did not reach statistical significance (SMD = 0.73, 95% CI: −0.05–1.50). High heterogeneity was observed ( I 2 = 90.4%, p < 0.001), indicating substantial variation in the reported effects across studies. This suggests that although SET may improve ADL, the evidence is not conclusive and requires further investigation (Figure 5 ). FIGURE 5 Forest plot illustrating the effect of SET on ADL in patients with stroke (ADL). Analysis of five studies showing overall effect size (SMD = 0.73, 95% CI: −0.05–1.50) with heterogeneity assessment ( I 2 = 90.4%, p < 0.001). 3.3.3. Lower Limb Motor Function Seven studies evaluated lower limb motor function using the FMA. The meta‐analysis demonstrated a significant improvement in the intervention group compared with controls (SMD = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.66–1.30, p = 0.042). Moderate heterogeneity was observed ( I 2 = 54.1%), suggesting some consistency in the beneficial effects of SET on lower limb motor function across studies (Figure 6 ). FIGURE 6 Forest plot depicting the effect of SET on lower limb motor function in patients with stroke as measured by Fugl‐Meyer Assessment (FMA). Analysis of seven studies showing overall effect size (SMD = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.66–1.30) with heterogeneity assessment ( I 2 = 54.1%, p = 0.042). 3.3.4. Balance Ability Three studies assessed balance ability using the FMB scale. The analysis showed a significant positive effect of SET (SMD = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.58–1.28) with low heterogeneity ( I 2 = 18.3%, p = 0.294). The individual study effects ranged from SMD = 0.69 to 1.22, with all studies consistently showing benefits from the intervention (Figure 7 ). FIGURE 7 Forest plot showing the effect of SET on balance ability of patients with stroke as measured by Fugl‐Meyer Balance (FMB). Analysis of three studies demonstrating overall effect size (SMD = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.58–1.28) with heterogeneity assessment ( I 2 = 18.3%, p = 0.294). 3.3.5. Walking Ability Three studies examined walking ability using the Holden functional walking rating. The meta‐analysis revealed a significant improvement in walking ability (SMD = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.61–1.50) with moderate heterogeneity ( I 2 = 44.8%, p = 0.163). The consistent positive effects across studies suggest that SET effectively improves walking ability in patients with stroke (Figure 8 ). FIGURE 8 Forest plot illustrating the effect of SET on walking ability of patients with stroke as measured by Holden functional walking rating. Analysis of three studies showing overall effect size (SMD = 1.05, 95% CI: 0.61–1.50) with heterogeneity assessment ( I 2 = 44.8%, p = 0.163). 3.3.6. Six‐Minute Walk Test Three studies evaluated walking endurance using the 6‐min walk test (6MWT). The pooled analysis showed a small, non‐significant effect favoring the intervention group (SMD = 0.15, 95% CI: −0.22–0.53) with no heterogeneity ( I 2 = 0.0%, p = 0.824). This suggests that although SET might have some positive impact on walking endurance, the effect is minimal and requires further investigation (Figure 9 ). FIGURE 9 Forest plot depicting the effect of SET on 6‐min Walk Test performance in patients with stroke. Analysis of three studies showing overall effect size (SMD = 0.15, 95% CI: −0.22–0.53) with heterogeneity assessment ( I 2 = 0.0%, p = 0.824). 4. Discussion The results of this systematic review and meta‐analysis indicate that SET has significantly positive effects in the rehabilitation process of patients with stroke, particularly in balance function, lower limb motor function, and walking ability. These findings provide strong support for SET as an effective rehabilitation intervention and offer important reference points for clinical practice and research in the field of stroke rehabilitation. The balance impairments commonly faced by patients with stroke not only increase the risk of falls but also severely affect their ADL and quality of life (Thayabaranathan et al. 2022 ). To address this, SET provides support through a suspension system, allowing patients to perform dynamic balance training in a relatively safe and controlled environment. This training method effectively stimulates the vestibular and proprioceptive systems of patients, promoting neural plasticity and functional reconstruction, thereby significantly improving patients' balance abilities (Huang et al. 2022 ). Additionally, SET can adjust the difficulty and intensity of training to meet rehabilitation needs at different stages, further enhancing the training effects (Kim et al. 2018 ). This personalized and adjustable feature makes SET highly flexible and adaptable in clinical applications, catering to the specific needs of different patients. After stroke, patients often experience lower limb muscle weakness and decreased motor control ability, leading to walking difficulties and limited activities (Tseng et al. 2022 ). SET alleviates the body weight burden, enabling patients to engage more effectively in lower limb training, thereby promoting the recovery of muscle strength and improvements in motor control ability (Mun et al. 2022 ). Research results show that patients receiving SET intervention scored significantly higher on the FMA than the control group, indicating that SET has a clear advantage in recovering lower limb motor functions. This finding is valuable for developing personalized rehabilitation plans, enabling clinicians to better address the specific needs of patients and formulate effective rehabilitation strategies. Walking ability is one of the key indicators for assessing functional recovery in patients with stroke, directly affecting their independence and quality of life. SET simulates natural gait and provides appropriate support, helping patients gradually restore gait stability and efficiency (Chen et al. 2023 ). Research results demonstrate significant improvements in the Holden functional walking rating after SET, indicating its strong potential in restoring patients' gait and walking efficiency. This not only helps patients regain the ability to walk independently but also enhances their ability to manage daily life, further improving their quality of life. However, this study also found that the effect of SET on improving ADL abilities did not reach statistical significance. This may be related to factors such as intervention duration, training intensity, or differences in assessment tools. For example, some studies had shorter training cycles, which might be insufficient to fully reflect the long‐term impact of SET on ADL. Additionally, ADL assessments involve multiple dimensions and are influenced by various factors, making it difficult for a single training intervention to significantly improve all aspects of ADL abilities. Future research could consider extending the intervention duration, increasing training intensity, or combining other rehabilitation methods to further explore the potential of SET in improving ADL. It is noteworthy that this study observed high heterogeneity in some results, indicating that there are differences among studies in terms of intervention methods, patient characteristics, and assessment indicators. This heterogeneity may arise from multiple factors, including the specific SET implementation methods, training frequency, and duration, as well as patients' stroke types, severity, and rehabilitation stages (Zhang et al. 2024 ). For example, different studies may vary in suspension height, training postures, and training content in SET, which can affect the intervention outcomes. Moreover, individual differences such as age, gender, and pre‐existing health conditions may contribute to the diversity of research results. Therefore, future studies should strive to develop more standardized SET intervention protocols, unifying intervention parameters and assessment standards to reduce heterogeneity among studies, thereby enhancing the reliability and comparability of meta‐analysis results (Long et al. 2022 ). Furthermore, the results of this study suggest that the effectiveness of SET may vary across different rehabilitation stages. In the early rehabilitation stage, when patients have higher neural plasticity, SET may be more beneficial for promoting neural function reconstruction and motor ability recovery; however, in the later stages of rehabilitation, SET may primarily serve to maintain and consolidate the achieved rehabilitation outcomes (Taye 2024 ). Therefore, developing personalized SET intervention protocols tailored to different rehabilitation stages may further enhance its rehabilitation effects. For example, in the early stage, SET can focus on promoting neural plasticity and functional reconstruction; in the late stage, SET can be more geared toward maintaining and consolidating motor functions and preventing functional regression. Another issue to consider is the combined application of SET with other rehabilitation methods. Although SET has produced notable effects when used alone, combining it with other rehabilitation methods, such as robot‐assisted gait training, virtual reality technology, or electrical stimulation therapy, may further enhance its effectiveness, providing more comprehensive and integrated rehabilitation support (Akıncı et al. 2023 ). For instance, combining SET with robot‐assisted gait training can simultaneously improve muscle strength and gait stability, and integrating SET with virtual reality technology can increase the fun and interactivity of training, enhancing patients' engagement and training outcomes. Additionally, combining SET with electrical stimulation therapy can enhance muscle strength while promoting neural function recovery, achieving better rehabilitation results. Therefore, future research should explore the combined application of SET with other rehabilitation methods to achieve more optimal rehabilitation outcomes. Another important finding of this study is that the impact of SET on 6MWT performance did not reach statistical significance. The 6MWT is a key indicator for assessing patients' walking endurance and functional status, reflecting the persistence of their walking ability in daily life. Although SET showed significant effects on other walking ability assessment tools, its effect on the 6MWT was small and did not achieve statistical significance. This may be related to several factors. First, the 6MWT primarily assesses walking endurance, whereas SET interventions may focus more on the quality and stability of walking ability rather than endurance improvement. Second, the intervention duration and training intensity may have been insufficient to significantly enhance patients' walking endurance. Additionally, small sample sizes and differences in study designs may affect the value of the results. Future research could design more specialized SET interventions targeting walking endurance, possibly combined with aerobic training methods, to achieve more significant effects on the 6MWT (Ebid et al. 2025 ). Despite the substantial effects of SET in stroke rehabilitation indicated by this study, the study's limitations must be acknowledged. First, although 23 RCTs were included, some studies had small sample sizes, which may affect the stability and generalizability of the results. Small sample sizes can lead to insufficient statistical power, increasing the risk of Type II or Type I errors. Additionally, there was a certain degree of publication bias in the studies, especially regarding some assessment indicators, which were not included in all relevant studies, potentially leading to biased results. Publication bias typically occurs when studies with significant results are more likely to be published, whereas studies with non‐significant results are less likely to be published, thus affecting the overall meta‐analysis results. Furthermore, the specific implementation details of SET, such as suspension height, training intensity, and frequency, varied across different studies, potentially influencing the comparability and integration of intervention effects. For example, some studies may have used higher suspension heights, providing more body weight support, whereas others may have used lower suspension heights, increasing the training load. These differences not only increase heterogeneity among studies but also may affect the interpretation and application of the results. Therefore, future research should implement stricter standardization in the specific SET implementation methods to reduce differences in intervention methods and enhance the comparability of research results. 5. Conclusion In summary, this study, through systematic review and meta‐analysis, has clarified the substantial effects of SET in the rehabilitation of patients with stroke, particularly in balance function, lower limb motor function, and walking ability. However, its impact on ADL requires further investigation. Future research should strive to develop more standardized SET intervention protocols, increase sample sizes, reduce study heterogeneity, and explore the combined application of SET with other rehabilitation methods to comprehensively enhance the rehabilitation outcomes and quality of life of patients with stroke. 6. Relevance for Clinical Practice The results encourage clinicians to include SET in stroke rehabilitation programmes, especially in the rehabilitation training of balance function, lower limb motor function, and walking ability, and flexibly adjust the training intensity and frequency of SET to the specific circumstances of patients to achieve improved rehabilitation results.
